transcript.text:
A fridge-freezer that is not cold can be caused by a setting or door not sealing, blocked air vents/over-packing, or an ice build-up stopping cold air reaching the fridge. If both sections are warm, a compressor or cooling-system fault becomes more likely. First, check the temperature setting is around 3–5°C for the fridge and -18°C for the freezer, with no holiday/eco mode selected, and make sure food is not blocking any internal vents. Is the freezer compartment still properly cold/frozen, or are both the fridge and freezer warm?
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
freezer still freezing fine. just the fridge part warm, milk going off

Because the freezer is still freezing, this is more likely to be a cold-airflow problem into the fridge than a complete cooling-system failure. The usual causes are a fridge setting or holiday/eco mode, food blocking the air vents, or ice build-up behind the freezer’s inner panel; a failed circulation fan is also possible. Please check the fridge is set around 3–5°C and that no holiday/eco mode is selected. Then move any food or packaging away from the vents, usually on the rear wall or near the top of the fridge. Is the setting/mode wrong, or are any vents blocked?
set to 3, freezer -19. nobody changed them. moved food from the back, no difference. hardly any air from the vents at back of fridge

This is now most likely either ice hidden behind the freezer’s rear panel restricting the airflow, or the internal circulation fan not running. Please look at the back wall/panel inside the freezer without removing anything: is there thick frost or ice there, rather than a light even dusting? Thick ice points to a defrost-system fault; no unusual ice makes the fan the more likely cause.
yes thick white frost on the back wall of the freezer, way more than I've ever seen. no burning smell or tripping btw

That heavy frost, combined with a freezer that still freezes and almost no air reaching the fridge, points to an ice blockage from a defrost-system problem. The likely failed component is within the automatic defrost system—commonly the defrost heater, sensor/thermostat or control/timer—but the ice can also stop the internal fan moving air. The useful next step is a full manual defrost: switch it off and unplug it, protect the floor with towels, move chilled/frozen food to cool boxes if possible, and leave both doors open until all ice has fully melted (often 24–48 hours). Do not chip ice with a knife or use a heat gun. Dry it, restart it and allow several hours for temperatures to recover. If airflow returns and the fridge cools again but thick frost comes back over the following days or weeks, that suggests an automatic defrost fault and it will need an appliance engineer to test and replace the failed defrost component. Check the freezer-door seal for a split, gap or section not sitting flat while it is defrosting, as a poor seal can also create excess frost.
ok will try the defrost. seals look fine, doors close properly. anything else to check meanwhile?

The only worthwhile extra owner check is the defrost drain once the ice has fully thawed. Look for the small hole or channel at the bottom of the freezer’s rear wall; if it is blocked, gently flush it with a little warm water or clear it with a soft pipe cleaner—do not use anything sharp. A blocked drain can add to ice problems, although the heavy frost and loss of fridge airflow still make an automatic defrost fault the main suspect. If the fridge recovers after defrosting but frosts up again, an engineer will need to test the defrost heater, sensor/thermostat and control system rather than replace parts by guesswork.

candidates: Cooling/airflow problem, such as blocked vents, heavy loading or a defrost-related ice build-up (medium)
Temperature setting, mode or door-seal issue (medium)
